questions.q: What is a Hugging Face model card, structurally?
options: A separate database record with no connection to the repo files
A repository's README.md file with a block of structured YAML metadata at the top
A PDF generated once when the model is first uploaded
A paid feature only available on enterprise accounts
questions.explain: Every model page is rendered from the repo's README.md — the prose below is for humans, and the YAML metadata block above it is what the Hub's search and filtering actually read.

options: It sets the model's file size limit
It only affects how the README is styled visually
It's the exact string transformers' pipeline(...) reads to know what task to run, and it's what makes a model show up when filtering the Hub by task
It's a required field with no functional effect
questions.explain: pipeline_tag connects three things at once: the rendered card, the Hub's task filter, and the actual code path pipeline(...) uses to load the right model class.

questions.q: What does the "self-reported" tag next to a model-index evaluation result mean?
options: The score was independently verified by Hugging Face staff
The score is fabricated and should be ignored entirely
The score came from whoever published the model, not an independent referee — a strong signal, not unconditional proof
The score only applies to paid models
questions.explain: model-index results are structured data the publisher supplies themselves. They're a real, useful signal, but they aren't independently audited, which is exactly what the self-reported tag flags.

questions.q: Why is a linked arXiv paper described as a "five-second credibility check"?
options: It guarantees the model is bug-free
Clicking through confirms the model implements a real, documented method, and "list models citing this paper" surfaces every other model built on the same approach
Papers are required by law for all public models
It replaces the need to read the model card at all
questions.explain: A paper link is a fast way to verify the method behind a model is real and traceable — and the citing-models list is a genuinely useful discovery tool for comparing alternatives.

questions.q: According to this lesson's checklist, why is no single signal (downloads, license, eval scores, lineage) sufficient alone when choosing a model?
options: Because the Hub removes models that fail any one check
Because only the first signal checked is ever accurate
Because each signal answers a different question, and strength in one (e.g. downloads) says nothing about another (e.g. license fit or benchmark performance)
Because signals contradict each other and cancel out
questions.explain: A high download count with no eval results, or strong eval results with a license that doesn't fit your use case, both leave you exposed — the checklist is meant to be read as a whole, not cherry-picked.
